blocks.text: A woman carries a heavy basin of water on her head through a crowded market and does not spill a drop. A tanker loaded with fuel takes the same corner and turns over. Both are about one point — the centre of gravity — and how far it sits above the ground.

blocks.title: Centre of gravity and centre of mass
blocks.text: The centre of gravity (CG) is the single point through which the whole weight of a body appears to act. The centre of mass is the point at which the whole mass appears to be concentrated. In the uniform gravitational field near the Earth's surface the two coincide, so at this level they are used interchangeably.

blocks.markdown: For a **uniform** body of regular shape the centre of gravity sits at its geometric centre. This single fact solves most beam and balancing questions.

rows: At the centre of the circle
Where the medians meet, two-thirds along each median from its vertex
At the centre of the sphere
At the midpoint of its axis
On the axis, h ÷ 4 above the base
blocks.caption: Centres of gravity of common uniform shapes

blocks.markdown:
### Locating the centre of gravity of an irregular lamina

Use the **plumb-line method**:

1. Make three small holes near the edge of the lamina.
2. Suspend it freely from a pin through the first hole and hang a plumb line from the same pin.
3. When both come to rest, draw the vertical line of the plumb line on the lamina.
4. Repeat from the other two holes.
5. The three lines intersect at the centre of gravity.

The method works because a freely suspended body always settles with its centre of gravity **vertically below** the point of support — otherwise the weight would exert a moment and keep turning it.

blocks.title: Centre of gravity of a loaded rod
blocks.prompt: A uniform rod of length 1.0 m and weight 20 N has a weight of 30 N firmly attached to one end. How far from that end is the centre of gravity of the whole system?

steps.text: The rod is uniform, so its own 20 N weight acts at its midpoint, 0.50 m from the loaded end.
Write the total weight of the system.
Take moments about the loaded end. The 30 N weight is at that end so its moment is zero.
Divide to find the position of the centre of gravity.
Sense-check: the CG has shifted from 0.50 m towards the heavier end, which is what we expect.

blocks.markdown:
### Three kinds of equilibrium

Displace a body slightly and watch what happens to the height of its centre of gravity.

- **Stable:** the CG **rises**, so gravity pulls the body back to its original position. A cone resting on its base.
- **Unstable:** the CG **falls**, so the body topples further away. A cone balanced on its point.
- **Neutral:** the CG stays at the **same height**, so the body simply stays where it is put. A sphere or a cone lying on its side on a horizontal table.

rows: Cone on its base; a bus with a loaded floor
Cone on its apex; a pencil balanced on its tip
Ball or cylinder rolling on a level table
blocks.caption: Comparing stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium

items: Lowering the centre of gravity increases stability — this is why a Bunsen burner has a heavy metal base.
Widening the base increases stability — racing cars are low and wide for exactly this reason.
A body topples when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base.
Loading a lorry high raises its centre of gravity and makes it topple more easily on a bend.
A double-decker bus is tested by tilting it fully loaded downstairs only, so that its CG stays low.

blocks.title: The CG need not be inside the body
blocks.text: The centre of gravity of a ring, a horseshoe or a boomerang lies in the empty space enclosed by the material. "Centre of gravity" describes where the weight effectively acts, not where any particular piece of matter is.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: When asked to explain stability, always give both parts of the answer: the position of the centre of gravity AND the area of the base. Answers mentioning only one of the two usually score half the available marks.

points: The centre of gravity is the point through which the entire weight of a body appears to act.
For a uniform regular body the CG is at the geometric centre; for a triangular lamina it is where the medians meet.
Find the CG of an irregular lamina by suspending it freely from three points and using a plumb line.
Equilibrium is stable if the CG rises on displacement, unstable if it falls, and neutral if its height is unchanged.
Stability is increased by lowering the centre of gravity and by widening the base; a body topples once the vertical through its CG leaves the base.
